work: Enarratio in Proverbia Salomonis regis Israel
source: Dionysii Cartusiani Opera Omnia, t. VII (Montreuil)

1.title: EXPOSITIO CAPITULI PRIMI : PARABOLÆ SALOMONIS.
1.title_en: Exposition of the first chapter: The parables of Solomon.

paras.t: Salomon tria nomina est sortitus : quoniam dictus est Salomon, quod interpretatur pacificus ; dictus est etiam Ecclesiastes, quod interpretatur concionator ; et iterum appellatus est Ididia, quod interpretatur amabilis Deo. Fecit quoque tria volumina, prætactorum nominum interpretationibus correspondentia. Etenim liber Proverbiorum correspondet nomini ejus, quod est Salomon, sive Pacificus : quia in libro Proverbiorum, de exercendis virtutibus, de vitiis evitandis, de spirituali profectu, de sapientiæ studio specialiter atque præcipue tractat : per quæ pax vera acquiritur et servatur, et homo Deo pacificatur. Liber autem Ecclesiastæ correspondet nomini ejus, quod est Concionator : quia in libro illo ad utramque partem argumentatur, et instar concionatoris in personis loquitur diversorum. Porro liber Cantici canticorum, nomini ejus, quod est Ididia, correspondet : quia in libro illo, de mutuo illo inter Sponsum et Sponsam ardentissimo purissimoque tractatur amore, per quem rationalis creatura fit Deo amabilis.
paras.en: Solomon was given three names: for he was called Solomon, which is interpreted “peaceable”[[1 Par 22:9||]] [the margin gives only Par. xxii; the name “Peaceable” is given at 1 Par 22:9]; he was also called Ecclesiastes, which is interpreted “preacher”[[Eccles 1:1||]]; and again he was named Ididia, which is interpreted “lovable to God”[[2 Kings 12:25||]] [the margin gives 1 Kings 12:3; the name is given at 2 Kings 12:25 (= 2 Samuel), where the Douay-Rheims has “Amiable to the Lord”]. He also made three volumes, corresponding to the meanings of the names just mentioned. For the book of Proverbs corresponds to his name Solomon, that is, Peaceable: because in the book of Proverbs he treats especially and above all of the virtues to be practised, of the vices to be avoided, of spiritual progress, and of the pursuit of wisdom; by which true peace is gained and kept, and man is set at peace with God. The book of Ecclesiastes corresponds to his name Preacher: because in that book he argues on both sides, and like a preacher speaks in the persons of different people. And the book of the Canticle of Canticles corresponds to his name Ididia: because that book treats of the mutual, most ardent and most pure love between the Bridegroom and the Bride, by which the rational creature becomes lovable to God.

paras.t: Præterea, quum philosophia sit triplex, scilicet ethica, logica et physica : liber Proverbiorum ad ethicam, id est moralem, reducitur, quoniam de virtutibus, præsertim moralibus, tractat ; liber vero Ecclesiastæ, ad logicam, quia scholastice et disputative procedit ; liber autem Cantici canticorum, ad physicam seu naturalem, quia ad Creatoris amorem, cœlestisque Sponsi internum amplexum, atque ad summæ et incomparabilis veritatis contemplationem universa natura, totusque ordo creaturæ dirigunt, excitant ac deducunt. Propter quod ait Apostolus : Invisibilia Dei, per ea quæ facta sunt, cognoscuntur ; sempiterna quoque virtus ejus et divinitas. Et Isaias exhortans : Levate, inquit, in excelsum oculos vestros, et videte quis creavit hæc.
paras.en: Moreover, since philosophy is threefold, namely ethics, logic and physics, the book of Proverbs is referred to ethics, that is, to moral philosophy, since it treats of the virtues, especially the moral virtues; the book of Ecclesiastes to logic, since it proceeds in the manner of the schools and by disputation; and the book of the Canticle of Canticles to physics, or natural philosophy, since the whole of nature and the entire order of creation direct, rouse and lead us to the love of the Creator, to the inward embrace of the heavenly Bridegroom, and to the contemplation of the supreme and incomparable truth. For which reason the Apostle says: [[Rom 1:20|the invisible things of him from the creation of the world are clearly seen, being understood by the things that are made|Invisibilia Dei, per ea quæ facta sunt, cognoscuntur]]; [[Rom 1:20|His eternal power also and divinity|sempiterna quoque virtus ejus et divinitas]]. And Isaias, exhorting us: [[Is 40:26|Lift up|Levate]], he says, [[Is 40:26|your eyes on high, and see who hath created these things|in excelsum oculos vestros, et videte quis creavit hæc]].

paras.t: Amplius, quum triplex sit status fidelium, puta incipientium, proficientium, et perfectorum : liber Proverbiorum magis coaptatur statui incipientium, quoniam liber hic tractat de vitiorum exstirpatione, de timore Dei, de disciplina, de correptione et correctione æquanimiter suscipiendis, de linguæ custodia, et consimilibus multis. Liber vero Ecclesiastæ magis convenire videtur statui proficientium, quoniam tractat de rerum transitoriarum vanitate, de instabilitate sæculi hujus, de accessu mentis ad unum invariabile bonum, de supergressione rerum inanium, et profectu virtutum, ac exercitatione in rebus divinis. Porro liber Cantici canticorum evidenter congruit statui perfectorum, quorum est per amorem ecstaticum, per viam unitivam, per limpidissimam contemplationem vacare et inhærere triumphantis ac militantis Ecclesiæ Sponso. Hæc autem per quamdam coaptationem, non per præcisionem sunt intelligenda. Non enim in libro Proverbiorum præcise agitur de pertinentibus ad incipientes : imo et de filiali et sancto timore, de sapientiali contemplatione, de generatione Verbi æterni, de virtutibus purgati animi aliqua interseruntur : quemadmodum et in Ecclesiaste quædam de pertinentibus ad incipientes dicuntur.
paras.en: Further, since the state of the faithful is threefold, namely of beginners, of the proficient, and of the perfect, the book of Proverbs is better suited to the state of beginners, since this book treats of rooting out the vices, of the fear of God, of discipline, of rebuke and correction to be received with an even mind, of guarding the tongue, and of many like things. The book of Ecclesiastes seems better to fit the state of the proficient, since it treats of the vanity of passing things, of the instability of this world, of the mind's approach to the one unchanging good, of rising above empty things, of progress in the virtues, and of exercise in divine things. And the book of the Canticle of Canticles plainly suits the state of the perfect, whose part it is, through ecstatic love, by the unitive way [that is, the third stage of the spiritual life, after the purgative and the illuminative, in which the soul is united to God], through most limpid contemplation, to be free for and to cleave to the Bridegroom of the Church triumphant and militant. These things, however, are to be understood as a certain fitting, not as a strict division. For in the book of Proverbs it is not only things belonging to beginners that are treated: rather, some things are also put in about filial and holy fear, about the contemplation that belongs to wisdom, about the generation of the eternal Word, and about the virtues of the purified soul; just as in Ecclesiastes too some things are said that belong to beginners.

paras.t: Præterea, quum Salomon fuerit Christi figura, præfata tria nomina Salomonis potissime congruunt Christo. Ipse namque est verus ille pacificus Salomon, qui per sanguinem crucis suæ reconciliavit nos Deo ; estque pax nostra, qui fecit utraque unum. Ipse quoque est Ecclesiastes seu Concionator, disceptans contra reprobos et pro electis. Ipse est Ididia, de quo Pater æternus : Hic est, inquit, Filius meus dilectus, in quo mihi bene complacui. Et sicut devotissimus ait Bernardus, Christus in hoc mundo fuit noster Pacificus, in judicio erit Ecclesiastes, in patria vero Ididia erit, ubi Sponsa perfruetur ejus amplexu plenissime in ferventissima caritate.
paras.en: Moreover, since Solomon was a figure of Christ, the three names of Solomon mentioned above fit Christ above all. For he is that true peaceable Solomon, who [[Col 1:20|through the blood of his cross|per sanguinem crucis suæ]] reconciled us to God; and he [[Eph 2:14|is our peace, who hath made both one|pax nostra, qui fecit utraque unum]]. He too is Ecclesiastes, or the Preacher, pleading against the reprobate and for the elect. He is Ididia, of whom the eternal Father says: [[Matt 3:17|This is|Hic est]], he says, [[Matt 3:17|my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased|Filius meus dilectus, in quo mihi bene complacui]][[Matt 17:5||]]. And as the most devout Bernard says, Christ in this world was our Peaceable One, at the judgement he will be Ecclesiastes, and in the fatherland he will be Ididia, where the Bride will enjoy his embrace most fully in most fervent charity.

paras.t: Denique liber iste Proverbiorum Salomonis adscribitur, non quod ipse immediate ediderit aut conscripserit librum, sed quoniam verba ab eo prolata, ministri ejus notaverunt et conscripserunt hinc inde in schedulis et membranis, quæ postea ab aliquo sapiente in unum collectæ sunt, non tamen ab uno solo. Et istud conjicitur ex eo potissime, quod infra præmittitur prologus iste atque præfatio, Hæ quoque parabolæ Salomonis, quas transtulerunt viri Ezechiæ regis Juda ; et item ex eo, quod infra habetur, Parabolæ Salomonis, etc. Sicque ab exordio hujus libri, usque ad illud capitulum exclusive, creduntur ab uno sapiente collectæ ; atque ab illo loco, usque ad capitulum vicesimum quintum exclusive, ab alio : et ab illo capitulo, usque ad finem libri, a tertio. Verum his objici potest, quod ipsemet Salomon de se ipso protestatur : Quum esset sapientissimus Ecclesiastes, docuit populum, et investigans composuit parabolas multas ; quæsivit verba utilia, et conscripsit sermones rectissimos ac veritate plenos. Si ergo quis vellet tenere istum librum, sicut et alios duos sequentes, esse a Salomone editum et conscriptum, potest adjicere quod idcirco decimo capitulo prologus ille præmittitur, quoniam Salomon longa mora et occupatione alia interveniente, ibi quasi de novo incepit : prologum vero, qui vicesimo quinto præmittitur capitulo, non esse a Salomone, sed ab alio quodam insertum, ad insinuandum quod parabolæ ab illo loco sequentes, fuerunt a sapientibus Ezechiæ regis communicatæ aliquibus aliis gentibus id cupientibus, in alia lingua : sicque ab illis vere dicuntur translatæ. Nam si eas solummodo, sicut prætactum est, ex membranulis redegissent in unum, aptius diceretur, Illæ quoque parabolæ Salomonis, quas collegerunt, quam, Quas transtulerunt, viri Ezechiæ. Verumtamen de hoc assertive nil dico. Amplius, qui affirmant librum istum ab aliis esse collectum, asserunt prologum primi hujus capituli, non a Salomone, sed a collectore horum primorum decem capitulorum esse præmissum.
paras.en: Lastly, this book of Proverbs is ascribed to Solomon, not because he himself directly published or wrote the book, but because his ministers noted down the words he spoke and wrote them here and there on slips and parchments, which were afterwards gathered into one by some wise man, though not by one alone. And this is conjectured above all from the fact that further on this prologue and preface is set at the head: [[Prov 25:1|These are also parables of Solomon, which the men of Ezechias, king of Juda, copied out|Hæ quoque parabolæ Salomonis, quas transtulerunt viri Ezechiæ regis Juda]]; and likewise from the fact that further on we have: Parables of Solomon, etc.[[Prov 10:1||]] [these words stand as a heading before Prov 10:1 in the Vulgate; they are not part of the verse in the Douay-Rheims]. And so from the beginning of this book up to that chapter, exclusive, they are believed to have been collected by one wise man; from that place up to the twenty-fifth chapter, exclusive, by another; and from that chapter to the end of the book, by a third. But against this it can be objected that Solomon himself declares of himself: [[Eccles 12:9|whereas Ecclesiastes was very wise, he taught the people|Quum esset sapientissimus Ecclesiastes, docuit populum]], and [[Eccles 12:9|seeking out, he set forth many parables|investigans composuit parabolas multas]]; [[Eccles 12:10|He sought profitable words, and wrote words most right, and full of truth|quæsivit verba utilia, et conscripsit sermones rectissimos ac veritate plenos]]. If then anyone wished to hold that this book, like the two others that follow it, was published and written by Solomon, he can add that the prologue is set before the tenth chapter because Solomon, after a long delay and other business coming between, began there as it were afresh; but that the prologue set before the twenty-fifth chapter is not Solomon's, but was inserted by someone else, to suggest that the parables following from that place were communicated by the wise men of King Ezechias to certain other nations who desired it, in another language; and so they are truly said to have been translated [*transtulerunt*, which the Douay-Rheims renders “copied out”] by them. For if they had only gathered them into one from the parchments, as was said above, it would more fittingly have been said, “These also are parables of Solomon, which the men of Ezechias collected,” than “which the men of Ezechias translated.” However, I say nothing on this point by way of assertion. Further, those who affirm that this book was collected by others assert that the prologue of this first chapter was set at the head not by Solomon, but by the collector of these first ten chapters.

paras.t: Attamen ea quæ tetigi, videntur confirmari verbis Hieronymi, protestantis : Tribus nominibus fuisse vocatum Salomonem, Scripturæ manifestissime docent : Pacificum, id est Salomonem, et Ididia, hoc est dilectum Domini, et Coheleth, id est Ecclesiasten. Itaque juxta numerum vocabulorum, tria volumina edidit : In Proverbiis parvulum docens, unde ad filium crebro dirigitur ac repetitur sermo : in Ecclesiaste vero virum maturæ ætatis instruens, ut nequaquam in rebus mundi se putet esse perpetuum, sed caduca et brevia esse universa quæ cernimus ; ad extremum vero, jam consummatum virum, et calcato sæculo præparatum, Sponsi jungit amplexibus. Hæc Hieronymus.
paras.en: Yet the things I have touched on seem to be confirmed by the words of Jerome, who declares: “The Scriptures teach most plainly that Solomon was called by three names: Peaceable, that is, Solomon; and Ididia, that is, beloved of the Lord; and Coheleth, that is, Ecclesiastes. And so, according to the number of his names, he published three volumes: in Proverbs teaching the little child, which is why the discourse is so often addressed to “my son” and repeated; in Ecclesiastes instructing the man of mature age, that he should by no means think himself lasting among the things of the world, but that all that we see is perishable and brief; and lastly, the man now perfected and prepared, having trodden the world underfoot, he joins to the embraces of the Bridegroom.” So far Jerome.

paras.t: Itaque in exordio prologi hujus innuitur, de qua materia in libro isto tractetur. Parabolæ Salomonis filii David, regis Israel. Porro parabola vocatur similitudo, quoniam in sermone parabolico intellectus verborum accipitur non immediate juxta verborum seriem, significantiam ac tenorem, sed juxta rem significatam per verba. Dicitur namque parabola, a παρά, quod est juxta, et βουλή, sententia, quia directe non sumitur sensus parabolæ juxta verba, sed juxta significata per ea : sicut infra per arborem seu per lignum vitæ designatur sapientia ; per ventrem, intellectus ; per rete, deceptio. Sicque liber iste vocatur liber Parabolarum, seu Parabolæ : non quod omnes ejus sententiæ et doctrinæ, seu verborum complexiones sint tales, imo in multis est simplex et planus, non parabolicus sensus ; sed quia frequenter parabolico utitur modo loquendi. Et quantum ad hoc, verum est quod asserit Glossa libri Proverbiorum : Non, ut simplices arbitrantur, habet patentia (id est manifesta) præcepta ac documenta, sed quasi aurum in terra absconditum, et nucleum in nuce conclusum ; et sicut in hirsutis castanearum operculis inquiritur fructus intus contentus, sic in Proverbiis altius inquirendus est sensus divinus. Denique, sicut ait Hieronymus, Hebræi hunc librum appellant Parabolas ; editio autem vulgata vocat eum Proverbia, sicque communiter nominant et allegatur. Et concordat ac convenit utraque appellatio ista. Quæ enim parabolæ nuncupantur, quia obscura sunt, proverbia quoque recte dicuntur, quia in ore loquentium sæpe versantur, memoriterque tenenda sunt. Demum proverbia interdum ita obscura sunt, ut apte dicantur parabolæ. Unde Salvator : Hæc in proverbiis locutus sum vobis. Est autem consuetudo sapientium, suis sermonibus admiscere parabolica verba, juxta illud Job, Addidit Job assumens parabolam suam ; et secundum illud Numerorum, Assumpta Balaam parabola sua, ait.
paras.en: And so at the beginning of this prologue it is indicated what matter is treated in this book: [[1:1|The parables of Solomon, the son of David, king of Israel|Parabolæ Salomonis filii David, regis Israel]]. Now a parable is called a likeness, since in parabolic speech the understanding of the words is not taken directly according to the order, meaning and drift of the words, but according to the thing signified by the words. For *parabola* is so called from *para*, which means “beside,” and *boulē*, “opinion” [Denis's derivation; the Greek word is *parabolē*, “a setting side by side”], because the sense of a parable is not taken directly according to the words, but according to what is signified by them: as further on wisdom is signified by a tree, or the tree of life[[Prov 3:18||]]; understanding by the belly[[Prov 22:18||]]; deceit by a net[[Prov 29:5||]] [the margin gives only chapters iii, xxii and xxix; the verses given here are those that fit]. And so this book is called the book of Parables, or the Parables: not because all its sentences and teachings, or combinations of words, are of this kind (indeed in many places the sense is simple and plain, not parabolic), but because it often uses the parabolic manner of speech. And as to this, what the Gloss on the book of Proverbs asserts is true: “It does not, as the simple suppose, hold open (that is, plain) precepts and teachings, but is like gold hidden in the earth, and a kernel shut up in a nut; and as the fruit contained within is sought in the bristly husks of chestnuts, so in Proverbs the divine sense must be sought more deeply.” Further, as Jerome says, the Hebrews call this book Parables, while the common edition calls it Proverbs, and so it is commonly named and cited. And both these names agree and fit together. For the sayings that are called parables because they are obscure are also rightly called proverbs, because they are often in the mouths of those who speak, and are to be held in memory. Moreover, proverbs are sometimes so obscure that they are fittingly called parables. Hence the Saviour: [[John 16:25|These things I have spoken to you in proverbs|Hæc in proverbiis locutus sum vobis]]. Now it is the custom of the wise to mix parabolic words into their discourses, according to that saying of Job: [[Job 27:1|Job also added, taking up his parable|Addidit Job assumens parabolam suam]][[Job 29:1||]]; and that of Numbers: Balaam, [[Num 23:18|taking up his parable, said|Assumpta Balaam parabola sua, ait]][[Num 24:3||]] [the margin gives Num. xxiii, xxiv; the words recur at Num 23:7, 23:18, 24:3 and 24:15].

paras.t: At vero, ad quid tendant parabolæ istæ, et quis sit finis et fructus earum, subjungitur. Ad sciendam sapientiam. Quasi dicat : Parabolæ hæ ordinantur ad obtinendam notitiam divinorum, et veram illuminationem in fide, ad cognoscendum rationes credendorum, quatenus, juxta exhortationem principis Apostolorum, parati semper simus ad satisfactionem omni poscenti nos rationem de ea, quæ in nobis est, fide et spe. Et disciplinam, id est, ad cognoscendum documenta ac præcepta moralia, per quæ dirigenda et gubernanda est vita humana ; vel, Disciplinam, id est morum compositionem, seu debitam peccati correctionem. Ad intelligenda verba prudentiæ, id est verba prudentialia, quæ procedunt ex vera interiori prudentia, quatenus ea audiendo addiscant atque proficiant, atque discernere queant quid ex vera, et quid ex ficta ac falsa prudentia proferatur ; ut non credamus omni spiritui, sed simus prudentes sicut serpentes, et simplices sicut columbæ. Nam quod veræ discretioni contrariatur, non est verbum prudentiæ.
paras.en: But to what these parables tend, and what is their end and fruit, is added next: [[1:2|To know wisdom|Ad sciendam sapientiam]]. As if to say: these parables are ordered to gaining knowledge of divine things and true enlightenment in faith, to knowing the reasons of the things to be believed, so that, according to the exhortation of the prince of the Apostles, we may be [[1 Pet 3:15|ready always to satisfy every one that asketh you a reason|parati semper simus ad satisfactionem omni poscenti nos rationem]] of the faith and hope which is in us. [[1:2|and instruction|Et disciplinam]], that is, to know the moral teachings and precepts by which human life is to be directed and governed; or, *instruction*, that is, the ordering of conduct, or the due correction of sin. [[1:3|To understand the words of prudence|Ad intelligenda verba prudentiæ]], that is, prudent words, which proceed from true inward prudence; so that by hearing them they may learn and make progress, and may be able to discern what is uttered from true prudence and what from feigned and false prudence; so that we [[1 John 4:1|believe not every spirit|non credamus omni spiritui]], but are [[Matt 10:16|wise as serpents and simple as doves|prudentes sicut serpentes, et simplices sicut columbæ]]. For what is contrary to true discernment is not a word of prudence.

paras.t: Et ad suscipiendam eruditionem doctrinæ, id est, ad complectendum et exsequendum informationem Scripturæ et eorum qui eam docent ac sermocinantur, quatenus dociles simus, et diligenter intenti ad verba doctrinalia sapientium, juxta illud Job : Qui me audiebant, exspectabant sententiam, et intenti tacebant ad consilium meum ; exspectabant me sicut pluviam, et os suum aperiebant quasi ad imbrem serotinum. Quidam per doctrinam intelligit doctrinales scientias, ut grammaticam, logicam, etc. Sed non videtur quod istæ parabolæ ad illarum eruditionem suscipiendam ordinentur ; sed eas tanquam adminiculatorias atque præambulas potius præsupponunt. Justitiam, et judicium, et æquitatem, id est, ad suscipiendum ac obtinendum virtutem justitiæ, per quam Deo exhibeamus quod ei tenemur, et judicium discretionis servemus, æquitatem quoque ad proximos custodiamus, habendo nos congruenter ad eos, temperando rigorem justitiæ per dulcorem clementiæ ex circumspecta discretione. Æquitas quippe est proprie quædam relaxata ac temperata justitia : quatenus sicut Deus in omni opere suo circa intellectuales creaturas, justitiam misericordiamque contemperat, juxta quod scriptum est, Universæ viæ Domini, misericordia et veritas ; ita et nos vestigia Creatoris sequentes, justitiam et misericordiam commiscere discrete discamus et enitamur. Hinc oravit vir sanctus ad Dominum : Bonitatem et disciplinam et scientiam doce me.
paras.en: [[1:3|and to receive the instruction of doctrine|Et ad suscipiendam eruditionem doctrinæ]], that is, to embrace and carry out the teaching of Scripture and of those who teach and preach it, so that we may be teachable, and diligently attentive to the words of teaching of the wise, according to that saying of Job: [[Job 29:21|They that heard me, waited for my sentence, and being attentive held their peace at my counsel|Qui me audiebant, exspectabant sententiam, et intenti tacebant ad consilium meum]]; [[Job 29:23|They waited for me as for rain, and they opened their mouth as for a latter shower|exspectabant me sicut pluviam, et os suum aperiebant quasi ad imbrem serotinum]]. Someone understands by *doctrine* the learned sciences, such as grammar, logic, etc. But it does not seem that these parables are ordered to receiving instruction in those; rather they presuppose them as aids and preliminaries. [[1:3|justice, and judgment, and equity|Justitiam, et judicium, et æquitatem]], that is, to receive and obtain the virtue of justice, by which we render to God what we owe him; and that we may keep the judgement of discernment, and preserve equity towards our neighbours, behaving fittingly towards them, tempering the rigour of justice with the sweetness of clemency out of careful discernment. For equity is properly a certain relaxed and tempered justice: so that, as God in all his works towards intellectual creatures tempers justice and mercy together, according to what is written, [[Ps 24:10|All the ways of the Lord are mercy and truth|Universæ viæ Domini, misericordia et veritas]], so we too, following in the footsteps of the Creator, may learn and strive to mingle justice and mercy with discernment. Hence the holy man prayed to the Lord: [[Ps 118:66|Teach me goodness and discipline and knowledge|Bonitatem et disciplinam et scientiam doce me]].

paras.t: Ut detur parvulis, id est pusillis et imperfectis ; vel, Parvulis, id est humilibus ; astutia, id est circumspectio sagax, non vulpina calliditas : ut sint oculati et solertes ad vitandum fraudes, pericula et ruinam, ne sub specie boni fallantur, nec excidant a simplicitate quæ est in Christo, nec in via Dei remissius agant. Et adolescenti scientia et intellectus addatur, id est, in donis Spiritus Sancti quæ scientia et intellectus vocantur, proficiat, de rebus creatis assidue melius ac melius sentiendo, et ea quæ fidei sunt, perspicacius intelligendo. Denique, sicut divinus Dionysius loquitur, idcirco Scriptura frequenter parabolice fatur, quatenus ipsa loquendi obscuritas fiat studiosis fructuosæ exercitationis materia atque occasio : per quam utique mens ipsa in sua consideratione acuitur, et proficit inquirendo, subtiliusque intelligit quod quærebat. Itaque bona ista astutia est parvulis necessaria, ut sciant sophismatum vitare versutiam, quum et Apostolus exhortetur, Videte ne quis vos decipiat per philosophiam et inanem fallaciam : sicque evitatis erroribus, in veritatis notitia crescant. Hinc sancta animalia Ezechieli in visione monstrata, erant undique oculata.
paras.en: [[1:4|To give|Ut detur]] [[1:4|to little ones|parvulis]], that is, to the small and imperfect; or, *to little ones*, that is, to the humble; [[1:4|subtilty|astutia]], that is, shrewd circumspection, not the cunning of the fox: so that they may be watchful and alert to avoid frauds, dangers and ruin, lest they be deceived under the appearance of good, or fall away from the simplicity that is in Christ, or grow slack in the way of God. And that [[1:4|to the young man knowledge and understanding|adolescenti scientia et intellectus]] may be added: that is, that he may make progress in the gifts of the Holy Ghost that are called knowledge and understanding, thinking ever better and better of created things, and understanding more clearly the things that belong to faith. Further, as the divine Dionysius says, Scripture often speaks in parables so that the very obscurity of the speech may become for the studious the matter and occasion of fruitful exercise, by which the mind is sharpened in its consideration, makes progress by inquiring, and understands more finely what it was seeking. So this good subtlety is necessary for little ones, that they may know how to avoid the craftiness of sophisms, since the Apostle too exhorts: [[Col 2:8|Beware lest any man cheat you by philosophy and vain deceit|Videte ne quis vos decipiat per philosophiam et inanem fallaciam]]; and so, having avoided errors, they may grow in the knowledge of the truth. Hence the holy living creatures shown to Ezechiel in the vision were full of eyes on every side[[Ezech 1:18||]][[Ezech 10:12||]].

paras.t: Hucusque prologus : quem tamen aliqui dicunt paulo post finiri, quum dicitur, Timor Domini principium sapientiæ. Sed potius hic finiri videtur, quum dicitur : Audiens sapiens, sapientior erit. Quæ verba præmittuntur, ad insinuandum quam salubre et fructuosum exsistat, verba sapientium audire ; et ne quis tam eruditum ac sapientem se arbitretur, ut verba sapientialia auscultare et perpendere dedignetur. Porro, quod tractatus hic inchoetur, Glossa quoque interlinearis fatetur. Et rursus in Glossa habetur : Pulchre Salomon a sapientia incipit, quoniam optione sibi data, sapientiam petiit et accepit. Itaque sapiens homo, audiens verba sapientiæ ac doctrinæ, crescit in sapientia, vel addiscendo quod ignoravit, vel id quod scivit clarius cognoscendo, vel ex ejus notitia ad alia consideranda tendendo. Hinc et Philosophus ait, quod auditus est sensus disciplinæ, quia audiendo instruimur. Visus tamen plurium rerum differentias ostendit. Dupliciter equidem acquirimus scientiam, secundum Philosophum : Primo, audiendo ab aliis : et quantum ad hoc, magis deservit auditus. Unde et Apostolus dicit : Fides est ex auditu. Secundo, personaliter inquirendo : et quoad hoc, magis confert visus.
paras.en: Thus far the prologue; though some say it ends a little later, where it says, [[1:7|The fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom|Timor Domini principium sapientiæ]]. But it seems rather to end here, where it says: [[1:5|A wise man shall hear, and shall be wiser|Audiens sapiens, sapientior erit]]. These words are set first to suggest how wholesome and fruitful it is to hear the words of the wise; and that no one should think himself so learned and wise as to disdain to listen to and weigh the words of wisdom. Moreover, that the treatise begins here, the Interlinear Gloss also acknowledges. And again in the Gloss we have: “Solomon fittingly begins with wisdom, since, when the choice was given him[[3 Kings 3:5||]], he asked for wisdom[[3 Kings 3:9||]] and received it[[3 Kings 3:12||]].” So the wise man, hearing words of wisdom and teaching, grows in wisdom, either by learning what he did not know, or by knowing more clearly what he knew, or by going on from knowing it to consider other things. Hence the Philosopher too says that hearing is the sense of learning, because we are instructed by hearing; though sight shows the differences of more things. For we acquire knowledge in two ways, according to the Philosopher: first, by hearing from others, and as to this hearing serves the more. Hence the Apostle too says: [[Rom 10:17|Faith then cometh by hearing|Fides est ex auditu]]. Secondly, by inquiring for oneself, and as to this sight contributes the more.

paras.t: Circa hæc asserit Glossa : Sapiens ostendit, neminem esse tam sapientem in hac vita, qui non possit sapientior esse etiam ex dictis minorum. Audivit regina Saba Salomonem, minor majorem, et sapientior rediit ; audivit Moyses socerum multo inferiorem, et sapientior factus est. Hinc in suis Proverbiis ait Cyrillus : Oportet semper addiscere, et in extremis horis fundum sapientiæ desiderabilius indagare. Sapientia namque est finis prudentis : et ob hoc, quanto huic fini sumus viciniores, tanto majori impetu ad ejus amplexum curramus. Motus enim virtutis, sicut et motus naturalis, in fine est fortior : sed et dum visus exterior senio ingrossatur, interioris oculi visus acuitur. Dignum quippe est, ut dum plus viget mentis judicium, disciplinæ plus operam impendamus.
paras.en: On these words the Gloss asserts: “The wise man shows that no one in this life is so wise that he cannot become wiser, even from the sayings of lesser men. The queen of Saba heard Solomon, the lesser the greater, and went back wiser[[3 Kings 10:6||]][[3 Kings 10:7||]]; Moses heard his father-in-law, who was far beneath him, and was made wiser[[Ex 18:19||]][[Ex 18:24||]].” Hence Cyril says in his Proverbs: “We must always be learning, and in our last hours search out the depth of wisdom the more eagerly. For wisdom is the end of the prudent man; and therefore the nearer we are to this end, the greater the eagerness with which we should run to embrace it. For the movement of virtue, like natural movement, is stronger at its end; and while the outward sight grows dim with age, the sight of the inward eye is sharpened. It is fitting that, the more the judgement of the mind is strong, the more effort we should give to learning.”

paras.t: Ex his innotescit, quam reprehendendi sunt quidam superbi et scioli, qui idcirco prædicatorum aut superiorum suorum documenta aut monita audire contemnunt aut renuunt, quia se ea scire præsumunt. Et intelligens gubernacula possidebit. Eruditi namque in Scripturis, in lege, in juribus, et qui se ipsos in primis bene intelligunt, emendant ac regunt, digni sunt alios gubernare, quum gubernare non sit nisi ad finem dirigere. Qui autem scit regulas juris divini, præcepta, canones Ecclesiæ, viarum pericula, vitiorum et tentationum remedia, atque veraciter prudens est, alios regere est idoneus. Propter quod Seneca dixit : Multos regere potes, si tu te rexeris ipse ; et denuo, Plurimos poteris gubernare, si te gubernet ratio recta. Hinc rector illitteratus rite vocatur asinus coronatus. Quis est intelligens, nisi cujus mentem passiones et vitia non excæcant ? Cæcus autem, hoc est homo passionatus, quamvis sit informi scientia plenus, si cæco ducatum præbeat, ambo in foveam cadunt. Ideo ait Glossa : Nemo de sua se jactet scientia. Qui sapientium verba audire negligit et implere, vitam suam gubernare non novit, multoque minus alienam. Hinc ait Philosophus : Homines ratione et intellectu vigentes, naturaliter aliorum domini sunt et rectores.
paras.en: From this it is clear how blameworthy are certain proud men and smatterers, who scorn or refuse to hear the teachings or warnings of preachers or of their superiors, because they presume that they know them already. [[1:5|and he that understandeth shall possess governments|Et intelligens gubernacula possidebit]]. For those learned in the Scriptures, in the law, in the canons, and who first of all understand, amend and rule themselves well, are worthy to govern others, since to govern is nothing other than to direct to an end. And he who knows the rules of divine law, the precepts and canons of the Church, the dangers of the ways, the remedies of vices and temptations, and is truly prudent, is fit to rule others. For which reason Seneca said: “You can rule many, if you have ruled yourself”; and again: “You will be able to govern very many, if right reason governs you.” Hence an unlettered ruler is rightly called a crowned ass. Who is the man that understands, if not he whose mind passions and vices do not blind? But the blind man, that is, the man ruled by his passions, though he be full of unformed knowledge [*informis*: knowledge not informed by charity], [[Matt 15:14|if the blind lead the blind, both fall into the pit|si cæco ducatum præbeat, ambo in foveam cadunt]]. Therefore the Gloss says: “Let no one boast of his own knowledge. He who neglects to hear and fulfil the words of the wise does not know how to govern his own life, and much less another's.” Hence the Philosopher says: “Men strong in reason and understanding are by nature the masters and rulers of others.”

paras.t: Animadvertet parabolam et interpretationem, id est, parabolicam locutionem diligenter attendet, ejusque expositionem et sensum exquiret, vel ab aliis audiendo, aut in libris legendo, aut propria investigatione scrutando ; verba sapientium : quoniam verba sunt signa et notæ interioris sapientiæ, quæ per verborum audientiam ab audiente acquiritur. Hinc in Ecclesiastico legitur : In medio presbyterorum sapientium sta, et ex corde verbis illorum conjungere. Et ænigmata, id est obscura dicta eorum. Tales fuerunt gloriosi Apostoli, quorum primus dixit ad Salvatorem : Edissere nobis parabolam istam. Porro sapientes interdum parabolicis ænigmaticisque utuntur sermonibus, quatenus veritas veletur indignis, et studiosi exercitentur utiliter. Hinc Christus ab Apostolis interrogatus, Cur in parabolis loqueris eis ? respondit : Ut audientes non intelligant. Unde in Ecclesiastico habetur : In proverbiis sapientium conversare, ab ipsis enim disces sapientiam et doctrinam.
paras.en: [[1:6|He shall understand a parable and the interpretation|Animadvertet parabolam et interpretationem]], that is, he shall diligently attend to parabolic speech, and shall seek out its explanation and sense, either by hearing from others, or by reading in books, or by searching through his own inquiry; [[1:6|the words of the wise|verba sapientium]]: since words are signs and marks of the inward wisdom which is gained by the hearer through hearing the words. Hence we read in Ecclesiasticus: [[Ecclus 6:35|Stand in the multitude of ancients that are wise|In medio presbyterorum sapientium sta]], [[Ecclus 6:35|and join thyself from thy heart|et ex corde]] to their words [the margin gives only Ecclus. vi; Denis has “in the midst of” and “to their words” where the Vulgate of Ecclus 6:35 has “in the multitude of” and “to their wisdom”]. [[1:6|and their mysterious sayings|Et ænigmata]], that is, their obscure sayings. Such were the glorious Apostles, the first of whom said to the Saviour: [[Matt 15:15|Expound to us this parable|Edissere nobis parabolam istam]]. Now the wise sometimes use parabolic and riddling discourses, so that the truth may be veiled from the unworthy and the studious usefully exercised. Hence Christ, being asked by the Apostles, [[Matt 13:10|Why speakest thou to them in parables|Cur in parabolis loqueris eis]]?, answered: That [[Luke 8:10|hearing may not understand|audientes non intelligant]][[Matt 13:13||]]. Hence we have in Ecclesiasticus: [[Ecclus 8:9|acquaint thyself with their proverbs|In proverbiis sapientium conversare]], that is, of the wise; [[Ecclus 8:10|For of them thou shalt learn wisdom, and instruction|ab ipsis enim disces sapientiam et doctrinam]].

paras.t: Timor Domini est principium sapientiæ. Hoc idem in Psalmo jam dictum fuit a patre Salomonis, dicente : Sanctum et terribile nomen ejus ; initium sapientiæ timor Domini. Quod potissime verum est de sapientia salutari infusa, quæ est donum Spiritus Sancti : quæ sine caritate et gratia non habetur. Itaque, quum sapientia ista in malevolam non introeat animam, recte asseritur quod timor Dei sit principium ejus, quoniam timor retrahit a peccatis, sicque ad infusionem sapientiæ præparat mentem. Et istud de timore pure servili est accipiendum. Nam timor filialis, imo et initialis, simul cum caritate et sapientia ista habetur. Timor vero pure servilis, a caritate et sapientia segregatur, quia non amat justitiam, sed pravitatem, quam non amore Dei, sed ex respectu supplicii vitat : et tamen ex ea parte, qua retrahit a peccato, disponit ad bona, et bonus est, quamvis non meritorius.
paras.en: [[1:7|The fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom|Timor Domini est principium sapientiæ]]. This same thing had already been said in the Psalm by Solomon's father, who says: [[Ps 110:9|Holy and terrible is his name|Sanctum et terribile nomen ejus]]; [[Ps 110:10|The fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom|initium sapientiæ timor Domini]]. This is true above all of saving, infused wisdom, which is a gift of the Holy Ghost[[Is 11:2||]], and which is not had without charity and grace. And so, since this [[Wis 1:4|wisdom will not enter into a malicious soul|sapientia ista in malevolam non introeat animam]], it is rightly asserted that the fear of God is its beginning, since fear draws us back from sins and so prepares the mind for the infusion of wisdom. And this is to be taken of purely servile fear [that is, fear of punishment alone]. For filial fear, and indeed initial fear [that is, fear partly of punishment and partly from love, the fear of beginners], is had together with charity and this wisdom. But purely servile fear is set apart from charity and wisdom, because it does not love justice but wickedness, which it avoids not out of love of God but out of regard for punishment; and yet, in so far as it draws back from sin, it disposes to good things, and is good, though not meritorious.

paras.t: Ideo ait Glossa : Duo sunt timores Dei : unus servilis, qui initium sapientiæ est ; alius amicitialis seu filialis, qui perfectionem sapientiæ comitatur. Servilis, principium est sapientiæ [ejus] qui post errata sapere incipit, et facit timere ne puniatur ; sed hunc perfecta caritas foras mittit. Succedit huic, timor Domini sanctus, permanens in sæculum sæculi : quem caritas non excludit, sed auget ; quo timet filius ne vel in modico oculos amantissimi Patris offendat. His verbis addit Glossa : Uterque in futuro cessabit. Contra quod objici potest, quod et anima Christi fuit et est plena timore hoc filiali, Isaia dicente : Replebit eum spiritus timoris Domini. Atque, ut alibi legitur, Exercitus cœli cum tremore adsistit ei. Propter quod cantatur in Canone : Tremunt Potestates. Et respondendum, quod timor filialis cessat et evacuatur in patria, quantum ad actum ejus qui est sollicitari ne peccando Deum offendat : quia Beati in gratia confirmati, sciunt se non posse peccare. Et quantum ad hunc actum, nunquam fuit in Christo timor filialis. Verumtamen timor iste manet in futuro, quantum ad actum suum qui est reverentialiter affici circa Altissimum, et ex intuitu infinitæ majestatis ipsius in parvitatem propriam resilire.
paras.en: Therefore the Gloss says: “There are two fears of God: one servile, which is the beginning of wisdom; the other friendly or filial, which accompanies the perfection of wisdom. Servile fear is the beginning of wisdom for him who begins to be wise after his errors, and it makes him fear lest he be punished; but this one [[1 John 4:18|perfect charity casteth out|perfecta caritas foras mittit]]. After it comes [[Ps 18:10|The fear of the Lord is holy, enduring for ever and ever|timor Domini sanctus, permanens in sæculum sæculi]], which charity does not shut out but increases; by which the son fears to offend, even in a small thing, the eyes of his most loving Father.” To these words the Gloss adds: “Both will cease in the life to come.” Against this it can be objected that the soul of Christ was and is full of this filial fear, as Isaias says: [[Is 11:3|he shall be filled with the spirit of the fear of the Lord|Replebit eum spiritus timoris Domini]]. And, as we read elsewhere, the host of heaven stands by him with trembling[[3 Kings 22:19||]] [3 Kings 22:19 has the host of heaven standing by the Lord, but not “with trembling”]; for which reason it is sung in the Canon: “The Powers tremble” [words of the Preface of the Mass]. And the answer is that filial fear ceases and is done away in the fatherland as to that act of it which is to be anxious lest one offend God by sinning: because the Blessed, confirmed in grace, know that they cannot sin. And as to this act there never was filial fear in Christ. Yet this fear remains in the life to come as to its act which is to be moved with reverence towards the Most High, and, at the sight of his infinite majesty, to shrink back into one's own littleness.

paras.t: Denique ad intelligendum ea quæ infra de timore copiose introducuntur, advertenda sunt quæ in tertia parte Summæ suæ scribit Dominus Antisiodorensis : Timor, inquit, initialis et filialis sunt ejusdem speciei, quamvis differant accidente. Sicut enim homo albus et homo niger sunt ejusdem speciei, tamen nullus homo albus est homo niger ; ita timor filialis et timor initialis sunt speciei ejusdem, tamen nullus timor initialis est filialis. Timor autem filialis quandoque dicitur possessive, ut dicatur timor filialis timor filiorum Dei : et sic non distinguitur timor filialis ab initiali. Quandoque autem dicitur timor filialis per similitudinem, timor quo timetur Deus timore illo quo filii timent patres, quando timent separari a patribus, solo timore vel amore, etiamsi nulla ex hoc eis immineat pœna. Et sic diversificantur isti timores. At vero timor initialis est, quo timemus Deum, partim intuitu pœnæ, partim amore gloriæ : et vocatur initialis, quia est primo incipientium. Perfecta quoque caritas dicitur foras mittere timorem initialem, quantum ad hoc quod respicit pœnam. His verbis addit hic doctor : Potest etiam dici timor initialis, quia est initium sapientiæ. Fides namque et timor proprie dicuntur sapientiæ initia, quoniam mundant cordis palatum a culpa. De fide etenim in Actibus habetur, Fide purificans corda eorum : et de timore in Ecclesiastico legitur, Timor Domini expellit peccatum. Timor etenim servilis, et fides, mundant ab essentia culpæ ; timor vero initialis, a reliquiis vitiorum : quia etsi quis sit a peccato purgatus, adhuc manent in eo reliquiæ peccatorum, scilicet difficultas bene agendi, obscuritas intelligendi, obligatio satisfaciendi : quas expellit timor initialis. Sicque corde purgato per fidem atque timorem, sentit dulcedinem Dei : quemadmodum causa febris cum reliquiis suis expulsa, sentit sanatus dulcedinem cibi. — Insuper, teste Philosopho, timor parit diligentiam, et facit hominem bene consiliativum, sicque disponit ad sapientiam.
paras.en: Further, to understand what is brought in at length below about fear, we must note what the lord of Auxerre [William of Auxerre, in his *Summa aurea*] writes in the third part of his Summa: “Initial and filial fear,” he says, “are of the same species, though they differ by an accident. For as a white man and a black man are of the same species, yet no white man is a black man, so filial fear and initial fear are of the same species, yet no initial fear is filial. Now filial fear is sometimes so called possessively, so that filial fear means the fear of the sons of God; and in this sense filial fear is not distinguished from initial. But sometimes filial fear is so called by likeness: the fear by which God is feared with that fear with which sons fear their fathers, when they fear to be separated from their fathers, by fear or love alone, even though no punishment threatens them from this. And in this sense these fears are different. Initial fear, on the other hand, is that by which we fear God partly in view of punishment, partly out of love of glory; and it is called initial because it belongs first to beginners. Perfect charity, too, is said to cast out initial fear[[1 John 4:18||]] in so far as it looks to punishment.” To these words this doctor adds: “It can also be called initial fear because it is the beginning of wisdom. For faith and fear are properly called the beginnings of wisdom, since they cleanse the palate of the heart from guilt. For of faith we have in the Acts, [[Acts 15:9|purifying their hearts by faith|Fide purificans corda eorum]]; and of fear we read in Ecclesiasticus, [[Ecclus 1:27|The fear of the Lord driveth out sin|Timor Domini expellit peccatum]]. For servile fear and faith cleanse from the essence of guilt, but initial fear from the remnants of vices: because even if someone has been cleansed from sin, there still remain in him the remnants of sins, namely difficulty in doing good, darkness in understanding, and the obligation of making satisfaction; and these initial fear drives out. And so, the heart being cleansed by faith and fear, it tastes the sweetness of God; just as, when the cause of a fever has been driven out with its remnants, the man who has been healed tastes the sweetness of food.” Moreover, on the witness of the Philosopher, fear gives rise to diligence and makes a man take good counsel, and so disposes to wisdom.

paras.t: Sapientiam, per quam contemplamur divina, et doctrinam, id est moralem scientiam, stulti despiciunt. In Scripturis, stulti dicuntur omnes homines vitiosi, carnales et imperiti, qui summo et invariabili bono præferunt transitoria, carnalia et caduca : in quibus regnat vitium puerilitatis, dono sapientiæ directe contrarium. Nam sicut pueri poma et pira præferunt auro ac gemmis, sic isti terrena et vana spiritualibus et æternis, ut scribit Guillelmus Parisiensis. Illi ergo sapientiam salutarem et doctrinam salubrem contemnunt : quia etsi verbis dicant se eas diligere, opere tamen negant. Et dato, quod pro adipiscienda informi sapientia ac doctrina scholastica studeant ac laborent, ad consequendum commoda et honores vitæ præsentis ; sapientiam tamen formatam, et scientiam actualem, boni approbativam, despiciunt, hoc est, non curant, nec apprehendere moliuntur. Imo quidam eorum sunt ita carnales et vani, quod eas irrident, nec appetunt. Tales fuerunt Scribæ et Pharisæi, qui Christum contra avaritiam prædicantem deriserunt, dicentes : Insanit : quid eum auditis ? Ideo protestatur Apostolus Corinthiis : Animalis homo non percipit ea quæ sunt Spiritus Dei ; stultitia enim est illi.
paras.en: [[1:7|Fools despise|stulti despiciunt]] [[1:7|wisdom|Sapientiam]], by which we contemplate divine things, [[1:7|and instruction|et doctrinam]], that is, moral knowledge. In the Scriptures all vicious, carnal and unskilled men are called fools, who prefer passing, carnal and perishable things to the supreme and unchanging good; in whom reigns the vice of childishness, directly contrary to the gift of wisdom. For as children prefer apples and pears to gold and jewels, so these prefer earthly and vain things to spiritual and eternal ones, as William of Paris writes. These, then, despise saving wisdom and wholesome teaching: because, though in words they say they love them, yet in deed they deny them[[Tit 1:16||]]. And granted that they study and toil to acquire unformed wisdom and the learning of the schools, so as to obtain the advantages and honours of the present life, yet they despise formed wisdom [that is, wisdom informed by charity] and practical knowledge that approves the good; that is, they do not care for them, nor strive to lay hold of them. Indeed some of them are so carnal and vain that they laugh at them and do not desire them. Such were the Scribes and Pharisees, who derided Christ when he preached against avarice[[Luke 16:13||]][[Luke 16:14||]], saying: He [[John 10:20|is mad. Why hear you him|Insanit : quid eum auditis]]? [the margin gives Joann. v… 20; the words are at John 10:20]. Therefore the Apostle declares to the Corinthians: [[1 Cor 2:14|the sensual man perceiveth not these things that are of the Spirit of God. For it is foolishness to him|Animalis homo non percipit ea quæ sunt Spiritus Dei ; stultitia enim est illi]].

paras.t: Præterea, sapientia, scientia, prudentia, de quibus in his Sapientialibus libris tractatur, sine virtutibus non habentur ; nec nuda notitia efficit sapientem : imo sciens et non faciens, pejor atque stolidior est ignaro. Ideo omnis stultus veram hanc sapientiam et doctrinam hanc practicam, cujus finis est bene conversari, contemnit. Et juxta hunc sensum Seneca in epistola loquitur : Illud ante omnia vide, utrum in philosophia, an in ipsa vita, profeceris. Philosophia non est artificium populare, nec ostentatione paratum ; non in verbis, sed in rebus est. Animum format et fabricat, vitam disponit, actiones regit, agenda et omittenda demonstrat ; sedet ad gubernacula, et per ancipitia fluctuantium dirigit cursum.
paras.en: Moreover, the wisdom, knowledge and prudence treated of in these Sapiential books are not had without the virtues; nor does bare knowledge make a man wise: rather, he who knows and does not do is worse and more foolish than the ignorant. Therefore every fool despises this true wisdom and this practical teaching, whose end is to live well. And in this sense Seneca says in a letter: “See above all whether you have made progress in philosophy or in life itself. Philosophy is not an art for the crowd, nor got up for show; it lies not in words but in deeds. It forms and fashions the soul, orders life, rules actions, shows what is to be done and what left undone; it sits at the helm and steers the course through the perils of those tossed by the waves.”

paras.t: Audi, fili mi, auribus cordis ac corporis, disciplinam, id est informationem et correptionem, patris tui : primo et maxime Patris cœlestis (cui quotidie in oratione dicimus, Pater noster, qui es in cœlis : ubi per Patrem tota superbeatissima Trinitas unus Deus intelligitur ; deinde etiam patris carnalis, cui in his quæ ad ejus auctoritatem ac præsidentiam spectant, est obediendum, dicente Apostolo : Filii, obedite parentibus carnalibus per omnia. Spirituali quoque patri, id est prælato, parere oportet ; maxime autem Patri æterno, quemadmodum ad Hebræos dicit Apostolus : Patres quidem carnis nostræ habuimus eruditores, et reverebamur eos : nonne multo magis obtemperabimus Patri spirituum, et vivemus? Et rursus ibidem : In disciplina perseverate ; tanquam filiis offert vobis se Deus. Et ne dimittas legem matris tuæ, id est militantis Ecclesiæ ; atque ad litteram per matrem videtur Synagogam intellexisse, quæ mater tunc exstitit Judæorum, sicut modo Ecclesia Christianorum. His verbis jubentur fideles omnem hæreticam atque schismaticam pravitatem abjicere, generalium quoque conciliorum canonibus obedire, et apostolicæ Sedi esse subjecti, ut solliciti sint servare unitatem spiritus in vinculo pacis.
paras.en: [[1:8|My son, hear|Audi, fili mi]] with the ears of heart and body [[1:8|the instruction|disciplinam]], that is, the teaching and the correction, [[1:8|of thy father|patris tui]]: first and above all of the heavenly Father (to whom we say daily in prayer, [[Matt 6:9|Our Father who art in heaven|Pater noster, qui es in cœlis]], where by "Father" the whole most blessed Trinity, one God, is understood); then also of the father in the flesh, who is to be obeyed in the things that belong to his authority and headship, as the Apostle says: [[Col 3:20|Children, obey your parents|Filii, obedite parentibus]] according to the flesh [[Col 3:20|in all things|per omnia]][[Eph 6:1||]]. One must obey the spiritual father too, that is, the prelate; but above all the eternal Father, as the Apostle says to the Hebrews: [[Heb 12:9|we have had fathers of our flesh for instructors, and we reverenced them. Shall we not much more obey the Father of spirits and live?|Patres quidem carnis nostræ habuimus eruditores, et reverebamur eos : nonne multo magis obtemperabimus Patri spirituum, et vivemus?]] And again in the same place: [[Heb 12:7|Persevere under discipline|In disciplina perseverate]]; [[Heb 12:7|God dealeth with you as with his sons|tanquam filiis offert vobis se Deus]]. [[1:8|and forsake not the law of thy mother|Et ne dimittas legem matris tuæ]], that is, of the Church militant; though in the letter he seems to have meant by "mother" the Synagogue, which was then the mother of the Jews, as the Church now is of Christians. By these words the faithful are bidden to cast away all heretical and schismatic wickedness, to obey also the canons of the general councils, and to be subject to the Apostolic See, so that they may be careful [[Eph 4:3|to keep the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace|servare unitatem spiritus in vinculo pacis]].

paras.t: Ut addatur gratia capiti tuo : id est, dona Spiritus Sancti, gratia gratum faciens, et virtutes infusæ augeantur in mente tua : quæ in cordibus obedientium solent perfici et augeri ; vel, gratia consummata, id est gloria sempiterna, addatur, ac detur cordi tuo in cœlo. Nam, ut ait apostolus Paulus, Gratia Dei vita æterna ; et item apostolus Joannes, De plenitudine ejus, videlicet Verbi æterni, omnes accepimus, gratiam pro gratia : quia ex gratia oritur ac procedit gratiæ incrementum, de habitu actus, de virtute merita, et tandem pro gratia meritoriæ actionis datur gratia, id est gloria beatificæ fruitionis. Et torques collo tuo. Torques est circulare et aureum ornamentum colli, quod capiti continuatur. Sicque per torquem potest contemplatio intellectus insinuari, quæ ex Deo conceditur, et in ipsum redit ac terminatur, et collum mentis pulcherrime ornat. Porro collum mentis, est vis prolativa verbi interioris. Quod autem contemplatio ista Dei recte per torquem notetur, constat ex eo, quod divinus Dionysius quarto capitulo de Divinis nominibus, contemplationem, quæ uniformis ac simplex est, comparat motui circulari.
paras.en: [[1:9|That grace may be added to thy head|Ut addatur gratia capiti tuo]]: that is, may the gifts of the Holy Ghost, sanctifying grace [that is, gratia gratum faciens, the grace that makes the soul pleasing to God], and the infused virtues be increased in thy mind, for these are wont to be perfected and increased in the hearts of the obedient; or, may consummated grace, that is, everlasting glory, be added and given to thy heart in heaven. For, as the apostle Paul says, [[Rom 6:23|the grace of God, life everlasting|Gratia Dei vita æterna]]; and likewise the apostle John: [[John 1:16|of his fulness|De plenitudine ejus]], namely of the eternal Word, [[John 1:16|we all have received: and grace for grace|omnes accepimus, gratiam pro gratia]]: because from grace arises and proceeds the increase of grace, from the habit the act, from virtue merits; and at last, for the grace of meritorious action, grace is given, that is, the glory of beatific enjoyment. [[1:9|and a chain of gold to thy neck|Et torques collo tuo]]. A torques [the Latin word for the chain of v. 9: a twisted ring of gold worn round the neck] is a round, golden ornament of the neck, which is joined to the head. And so by the chain can be signified the contemplation of the intellect, which is granted by God, returns to him and ends in him, and most beautifully adorns the neck of the mind. Now the neck of the mind is the power that utters the inner word. That this contemplation of God is rightly signified by a chain is plain from this, that the divine Dionysius, in the fourth chapter of the Divine Names, compares contemplation, which is uniform and simple, to circular motion.

paras.t: Consequenter docemur adulatione non vinci nec allici, nec aliorum instigatione ad vitia trahi, nec innocentibus adversari, sed pravam jugiter societatem vitare. Fili mi, si te lactaverint, id est, blandis sermonibus mulserint, peccatores, ne acquiescas eis in rebus illicitis, nec eorum adulatione delecteris, aut extollaris. Unde in Psalmo : Oleum peccatoris non impinguet caput meum. Seneca quoque in suis Proverbiis loquitur: Habet suum venenum blanda oratio. Quæ quam nociva sit ac repellenda, Dominus pandit, dicens : Popule meus, qui te beatum dicunt, ipsi te decipiunt, et viam gressuum tuorum dissipant.
paras.en: Next we are taught not to be overcome or enticed by flattery, nor drawn into vice by the urging of others, nor to set ourselves against the innocent, but always to shun wicked company. [[1:10|My son, if|Fili mi, si]] [[1:10|sinners|peccatores]] [[1:10|shall entice thee|te lactaverint]], that is, soothe thee with smooth words [lactare is literally "to suckle", hence to coax or cajole], [[1:10|consent not to them|ne acquiescas eis]] in unlawful things, nor take delight in their flattery or be puffed up by it. Hence in the Psalm: let not [[Ps 140:5|the oil of the sinner fatten my head|Oleum peccatoris non impinguet caput meum]]. Seneca too says in his Proverbs: Smooth speech has its own poison. How harmful it is and how it is to be repelled, the Lord shows, saying: [[Is 3:12|O my people, they that call thee blessed, the same deceive thee, and destroy the way of thy steps|Popule meus, qui te beatum dicunt, ipsi te decipiunt, et viam gressuum tuorum dissipant]].

paras.t: Si dixerint : Veni nobiscum mentis consensu, aut corporis gressu ; insidiemur sanguini, id est hominibus, ad effundendum eorum sanguinem, quatenus bona eorum diripiamus ; abscondamus, id est, occulte ponamus, tendiculas, id est nocendi laqueos, contra insontem frustra, id est ad persequendum innocentem ac justum sine rationabili causa. Quod faciendo iniqui imitantur caput suum diabolum, juxta illud beati Job : Abscondita est in terra pedica ejus, et decipula illius super semitam.
paras.en: [[1:11|If they shall say: Come with us|Si dixerint : Veni nobiscum]] by consent of mind or by the step of the body; [[1:11|let us lie in wait for blood|insidiemur sanguini]], that is, for men, to shed their blood, so that we may plunder their goods; [[1:11|let us hide|abscondamus]], that is, set in secret, [[1:11|snares|tendiculas]], that is, nooses to do harm, [[1:11|for the innocent without cause|contra insontem frustra]], that is, to persecute the innocent and just man without any reasonable cause. In doing this the wicked imitate their head, the devil, according to that of blessed Job: [[Job 18:10|A gin is hidden for him in the earth, and his trap upon the path|Abscondita est in terra pedica ejus, et decipula illius super semitam]].

paras.t: Deglutiamus eum sicut infernus viventem, id est, eum totaliter exstinguamus, et bona ipsius devoremus : sicut infernus deglutivit Dathan et Abiron viventes ; et integrum, quasi descendentem in lacum : id est, nihil relinquamus de eo residuum, sicut de eo qui in profundam labitur foveam, nil apparet. Unde in Jeremia populus Israel loquitur de rege Babylonis : Absorbuit me quasi draco, replevit teneritudine mea ventrem suum, posuit in lacum vitam meam. Omnem pretiosam substantiam reperiemus, id est, copiam divitiarum acquiremus ab his, quos ita oppresserimus ; implebimus domos nostras spoliis occisorum. Sortem mitte nobiscum, quis quid et quantum de præda accipiat : marsupium unum sit omnium nostrum, id est, omnia spolia ponamus in uno communi repositorio, ut postea ea inter nos dividamus.
paras.en: [[1:12|Let us swallow him up alive like hell|Deglutiamus eum sicut infernus viventem]], that is, let us destroy him utterly and devour his goods, as hell swallowed up Dathan and Abiron alive[[Num 16:33||]]; [[1:12|and whole as one that goeth down into the pit|et integrum, quasi descendentem in lacum]]: that is, let us leave nothing of him remaining, as nothing is seen of one who slips into a deep pit. Hence in Jeremias the people of Israel says of the king of Babylon: [[Jer 51:34|he hath swallowed me up like a dragon, he hath filled his belly with my delicate meats|Absorbuit me quasi draco, replevit teneritudine mea ventrem suum]], he hath put my life in the pit[[Lam 3:53||]] [these last words are from Lam 3:53, "My life is fallen into the pit", which the margin cites beside Jer 51:34]. [[1:13|We shall find all precious substance|Omnem pretiosam substantiam reperiemus]], that is, we shall get a store of riches from those whom we have thus oppressed; [[1:13|we shall fill our houses with spoils|implebimus domos nostras spoliis]] of the slain. [[1:14|Cast in thy lot with us|Sortem mitte nobiscum]], as to who takes what and how much of the booty: [[1:14|let us all have one purse|marsupium unum sit omnium nostrum]], that is, let us put all the spoils in one common store, so as to divide them among us afterwards.

paras.t: Istud ad litteram de latronibus ac furibus, atque raptoribus generaliter potest intelligi, qui vitam naturæ et exteriora auferunt bona : de quibus in Job multa dicuntur. Atque apud Michæam Dominus ait : Comederunt carnem populi mei, et pellem eorum desuper excoriaverunt. Porro tropologice accipi potest de hæreticis et seductoribus ceteris : qui vere catholicos ac devotos conantur subvertere, et suis implicare erroribus, per argumentationes ac suggestiones pestiferas : sicque spirituales eorum divitias, virtutes ac merita, et innocentiæ gratiam ipsis nituntur auferre. De quibus Dominus in Evangelio ait : Quotquot venerunt, fures sunt et latrones. Isti student conventicula sua augere, et domos suas implere personis Catholicorum, et animabus fidelium, quas potuerint fallere : ad quod agendum etiam ab invisibilibus hostibus instigantur. Allegorice vero exponuntur ista de Christo : quem sacerdotes, Scribæ, ac Pharisæi innocentem sunt persecuti ; cui varias posuerunt insidias. Et non solum ejus personam crudelissime occiderunt, sed memoriam quoque ipsius tollere tentaverunt, juxta illud : Eradamus eum de terra viventium, et nomen ejus non memoretur ultra. Nec solum Christum, sed et ejus discipulos pariformiter tractaverunt. Hinc Dominus in Psalmo ait de illis : Posuerunt me in lacu inferiori ; æstimatus sum cum descendentibus in lacum. Et ad Hebræos conversos scribit Apostolus : Rapinam bonorum vestrorum cum gaudio suscepistis.
paras.en: In the letter this can be understood of robbers, thieves and plunderers in general, who take away the life of nature and outward goods; of whom many things are said in Job[[Job 24:2||]]. And in Micheas the Lord says: [[Mich 3:3|Who have eaten the flesh of my people, and have flayed their skin off them|Comederunt carnem populi mei, et pellem eorum desuper excoriaverunt]]. Tropologically [that is, in the moral sense], it can be taken of heretics and the other seducers, who strive to overthrow true Catholics and devout people and to entangle them in their errors by pestilent arguments and suggestions, and so try to take from them their spiritual riches, their virtues and merits, and the grace of innocence. Of whom the Lord says in the Gospel: [[John 10:8|as many as have come, are thieves and robbers|Quotquot venerunt, fures sunt et latrones]]. These are eager to enlarge their conventicles, and to fill their houses with the persons of Catholics and the souls of the faithful whom they have been able to deceive; and to do this they are also urged on by invisible enemies. Allegorically, however, these things are explained of Christ, whom the priests, Scribes and Pharisees persecuted, innocent as he was, and for whom they laid divers snares. And not only did they most cruelly kill his person, but they also tried to take away his memory, according to that: Let us [[Jer 11:19|cut him off from the land of the living, and let his name be remembered no more|Eradamus eum de terra viventium, et nomen ejus non memoretur ultra]]. And not Christ only, but his disciples too they treated in like manner. Hence the Lord says of them in the Psalm: [[Ps 87:7|They have laid me in the lower pit|Posuerunt me in lacu inferiori]]; [[Ps 87:5|I am counted among them that go down to the pit|æstimatus sum cum descendentibus in lacum]]. And the Apostle writes to the converted Hebrews: [[Heb 10:34|took with joy the being stripped of your own goods|Rapinam bonorum vestrorum cum gaudio suscepistis]].

paras.t: Hortatur itaque Salomon omnem Synagogæ filium, ne impiissimis illis consentiat. Fili mi, ne ambules cum eis, id est, nec corporaliter gradiaris cum talibus ad male agendum, nec spiritualiter, per consensum, aut alio modo eis communicando in vitiis. Prohibe pedem tuum a semitis eorum, ut nec corporeo progressu, nec aliquo inordinato affectu eis associeris in crimine. Pedes enim illorum ad malum currunt : quia ex malignitatis suæ affectu, non solum vadunt, sed etiam currunt ad scelera perpetranda : quod faciendo, currunt quoque ad æterna supplicia, quibus tam graviter excedendo propinquant. Et festinant ut effundant sanguinem, non pensantes, nec formidantes quod Dominus ait : Quicumque effuderit sanguinem humanum, effundetur sanguis illius, ad imaginem quippe Dei factus est homo : et quod ait Judex cœlestis, Omnis qui acceperit gladium, gladio peribit. Propria etenim iniquitate, quam gladio male utens committit, perit in anima et condemnari meretur : magisque nocet sibi quam alteri. Propter quod subditur :
paras.en: So Solomon exhorts every son of the Synagogue not to consent to those most wicked men. [[1:15|My son, walk not thou with them|Fili mi, ne ambules cum eis]], that is, neither go bodily with such men to do evil, nor spiritually, by consent or by sharing with them in their vices in any other way. [[1:15|restrain thy foot from their paths|Prohibe pedem tuum a semitis eorum]], so that thou be joined with them in crime neither by bodily going nor by any disordered affection. [[1:16|For their feet run to evil|Pedes enim illorum ad malum currunt]]: because from the affection of their malice they not only go but even run to commit crimes; and in doing so they run also to the everlasting punishments, which they draw near to by sinning so grievously. [[1:16|and make haste to shed blood|Et festinant ut effundant sanguinem]], not weighing nor fearing what the Lord says: [[Gen 9:6|Whosoever shall shed man's blood, his blood shall be shed: for man was made to the image of God|Quicumque effuderit sanguinem humanum, effundetur sanguis illius, ad imaginem quippe Dei factus est homo]]; and what the heavenly Judge says: [[Matt 26:52|all that take the sword shall perish with the sword|Omnis qui acceperit gladium, gladio peribit]]. For by his own iniquity, which he commits by using the sword ill, he perishes in his soul and deserves to be condemned, and he harms himself more than the other. Therefore it is added:

paras.t: Frustra autem jacitur rete, id est, laqueus circumventionis, prava doctrina, pestifera suggestio, persecutionis molestia inaniter extenditur, ante oculos pennatorum, id est coram sapientibus et virtuosis hominibus : qui interioris visionis acumine talia machinamenta faciliter deprehendunt, evadunt et vincunt ; adversa quoque, amore Dei ac futuræ felicitatis intuitu, æquanimiter patiuntur. Quorum corda virtutibus sunt alata, quibus volant in cœlum, desiderando æterna, quorum appretiatione parvi pendunt transitoria cuncta, tam prospera quam adversa, cum Apostolo protestantes : Id quod in præsenti est momentaneum et leve tribulationis nostræ, supra modum in sublimitate æternum gloriæ pondus operatur in nobis, non contemplantibus nobis ea quæ videntur, sed quæ non videntur. De quibus loquitur Isaias : Qui sperant in Domino, mutabunt fortitudinem, assument pennas ut aquilæ, volabunt, et non deficient. Hinc erepti ac triumphantes, grata ac hilari voce concinunt : Laqueus contritus est, et nos liberati sumus.
paras.en: [[1:17|But a net is spread in vain|Frustra autem jacitur rete]], that is, the noose of entrapment, wicked doctrine, pestilent suggestion, the trouble of persecution, is stretched out to no purpose, [[1:17|before the eyes of them that have wings|ante oculos pennatorum]], that is, in the sight of wise and virtuous men, who by the keenness of their inner sight easily detect such contrivances, escape them and overcome them, and also bear adversities with an even mind, for the love of God and with an eye to the happiness to come. Their hearts are winged with virtues, by which they fly to heaven, desiring eternal things; and by the value they set on these they hold all passing things cheap, prosperous and adverse alike, declaring with the Apostle: [[2 Cor 4:17|that which is at present momentary and light of our tribulation worketh for us above measure, exceedingly an eternal weight of glory|Id quod in præsenti est momentaneum et leve tribulationis nostræ, supra modum in sublimitate æternum gloriæ pondus operatur in nobis]], [[2 Cor 4:18|While we look not at the things which are seen, but at the things which are not seen|non contemplantibus nobis ea quæ videntur, sed quæ non videntur]] [the margin gives I Cor. iv, 18; the passage is 2 Cor 4:17–18]. Of whom Isaias says: [[Is 40:31|they that hope in the Lord shall renew their strength, they shall take wings as eagles|Qui sperant in Domino, mutabunt fortitudinem, assument pennas ut aquilæ]], they shall fly, [[Is 40:31|and not faint|et non deficient]] [Denis reads volabunt, "they shall fly", for the Vulgate's "they shall run and not be weary, they shall walk"]. Hence, rescued and triumphant, they sing with a glad and joyful voice: [[Ps 123:7|The snare is broken, and we are delivered|Laqueus contritus est, et nos liberati sumus]].

paras.t: Ipsi quoque contra sanguinem suum insidiantur : id est, insidiæ quas aliis parant, frequenter redundant in ipsos, et pro suis sceleribus temporali morte plectuntur, juxta illud in Threnis : Reddes eis vicem, Domine, juxta opera manuum suarum. Et moliuntur fraudes, id est, alios student decipere, contra animas suas, id est contra propriarum animarum salutem, quoniam suis fraudulentiis damnationem merentur æternam. Ideo ait Salvator : In qua mensura mensi fueritis, remetietur vobis. Unde per Malachiam loquitur Dominus : Maledictus dolosus. Et Isaias : Fraudulenti, inquit, vasa pessima sunt. Denique tales affligunt se ipsos, et pace interna ac vera securitate se privant, quia quod aliis machinantur aut intulerunt, sibi quoque parari et inferri verentur. Sicque iniquus variis suspicionibus, angustiis, atque terroribus intra se premitur ac mordetur, juxta illud : Sonitus terroris semper in auribus impii, et quum pax sit, ille insidias suspicatur. Hinc Seneca in suis testatur Proverbiis : Res vera est : qui a multis timetur, multos timet. Itemque : Nequitia ipsa, pœna sui est; nam mala conscientia nunquam est secura. Cyrillus quoque in libro suorum fatetur Proverbiorum : Si quemquam offenderis, pavesce semper hujusmodi. Nam ubi offensæ memoria, ibi ira ; ira autem cupit vindictam, vindicta parit fraudulentiam, quæ serpit ad pœnam.
paras.en: [[1:18|And they themselves lie in wait for their own blood|Ipsi quoque contra sanguinem suum insidiantur]]: that is, the snares they lay for others often recoil upon themselves, and for their crimes they are punished with temporal death, according to that in Lamentations: [[Lam 3:64|Thou shalt render them a recompense, O Lord, according to the works of their hands|Reddes eis vicem, Domine, juxta opera manuum suarum]]. [[1:18|and practise deceits|Et moliuntur fraudes]], that is, they are eager to deceive others, [[1:18|against their own souls|contra animas suas]], that is, against the salvation of their own souls, since by their frauds they deserve eternal damnation. Therefore the Saviour says: [[Matt 7:2|with what measure you mete, it shall be measured to you again|In qua mensura mensi fueritis, remetietur vobis]]. Hence the Lord speaks by Malachias: [[Mal 1:14|Cursed is the deceitful man|Maledictus dolosus]]. And Isaias: [[Is 32:7|The vessels of the deceitful|Fraudulenti]], he says, [[Is 32:7|are most wicked|vasa pessima sunt]]. Lastly, such men afflict themselves, and rob themselves of inner peace and true security, because what they contrive against others or have done to them, they fear will be prepared and done to them too. And so the wicked man is pressed and gnawed within by divers suspicions, anxieties and terrors, according to that: [[Job 15:21|The sound of dread is always in his ears: and when there is peace, he always suspecteth treason|Sonitus terroris semper in auribus impii, et quum pax sit, ille insidias suspicatur]]. Hence Seneca testifies in his Proverbs: It is a true thing: he who is feared by many, fears many. And again: Wickedness is its own punishment, for a bad conscience is never secure. Cyril too declares in the book of his Proverbs: If thou hast offended anyone, be ever afraid of him. For where there is the memory of an offence, there is anger; and anger desires vengeance, vengeance breeds fraud, which creeps on to punishment.

paras.t: Sic semitæ omnis avari, id est excogitationes et practicæ hominum avarorum, animas possidentium rapiunt, id est, ipsas animas cupidorum possidentium aliena sive superflua, pertrahunt ad gehennalia tormenta. Ideo scriptum est : Dives quum dormierit, nihil secum auferet ; apprehendet eum quasi aqua inopia. Ideo Seneca asserit : Avarus nil rectum facit, nisi dum moritur. Quia videlicet tunc relinquit quæ injuste detinuit, et debitam recipit pœnam. De his damnabilibus semitis cupidorum profert Cyrillus : Totum officium opulentiæ mundialis, in tribus assiduis vitiis, et in uno continuo tormento consistit, videlicet in insatiabili cupiditate, in inquieta rapacitate, in incessabili illiberalitate, et in timiditate perpetua. Recte ergo locutus est Isaias : Væ qui conjungitis domum ad domum, et agrum agro copulatis ; atque Apostolus, Qui volunt divites fieri, incidunt in tentationem et laqueum diaboli, et in desideria multa inutilia, quæ mergunt hominem in interitum et perditionem. Præterea verbum hoc præinductum aliqui sic exponunt : Semitæ omnis avari animas possidentium rapiunt, id est, eos qui rebus terrenis abundant, spoliare conantur.
paras.en: [[1:19|So the ways of every covetous man|Sic semitæ omnis avari]], that is, the schemes and practices of covetous men, [[1:19|destroy the souls of the possessors|animas possidentium rapiunt]], that is, they drag the very souls of the greedy, who possess what belongs to others or what is superfluous, to the torments of hell [rapiunt is literally "snatch away"]. Therefore it is written: [[Job 27:19|The rich man when he shall sleep shall take away nothing with him|Dives quum dormierit, nihil secum auferet]]; [[Job 27:20|Poverty like water shall take hold on him|apprehendet eum quasi aqua inopia]]. Therefore Seneca asserts: The miser does nothing right except when he dies: because then, namely, he leaves what he held unjustly and receives the punishment due. Of these damnable ways of the greedy Cyril says: The whole business of worldly wealth consists in three constant vices and one continual torment: namely in insatiable greed, in restless rapacity, in unceasing meanness, and in perpetual fearfulness. Rightly then did Isaias say: [[Is 5:8|Woe to you that join house to house and lay field to field|Væ qui conjungitis domum ad domum, et agrum agro copulatis]]; and the Apostle: [[1 Tim 6:9|they that will become rich fall into temptation and into the snare of the devil and into many unprofitable and hurtful desires, which drown men into destruction and perdition|Qui volunt divites fieri, incidunt in tentationem et laqueum diaboli, et in desideria multa inutilia, quæ mergunt hominem in interitum et perditionem]]. Further, some explain the words just quoted thus: [[1:19|the ways of every covetous man destroy the souls of the possessors|Semitæ omnis avari animas possidentium rapiunt]], that is, they try to rob those who abound in earthly goods.

paras.t: Consequenter ostenditur, neminem de suæ infidelitatis posse ignorantia excusari. Sapientia foris prædicat. Hoc de increata Sapientia, quæ est Christus Dominus, Dei Patris Verbum æternum, accipi potest : qui foris, id est inter gentiles ac perfidos, prædicavit. De quibus Apostolus : Quid mihi, inquit, de his qui foris sunt, judicare ? Hoc quippe Salvator in primo suo adventu per se aliqualiter adimplevit, in Decapoli, et Tyriis ac Sidoniis evangelizando, ut patet ex Evangelio. Denique ab exordio, per quosdam Patriarchas et Prophetas, annuntiavit multis gentibus viam salutis. Atque post suam resurrectionem, per Apostolos aliosque discipulos toti mundo legem evangelicam patefecit : quibus præcepit, Euntes in mundum universum, prædicate Evangelium omni creaturæ ; et item, Eritis mihi testes in omni Judæa et Galilæa, et usque ad ultimum terræ. Prædicavit etiam foris, id est manifeste in populo, quemadmodum testatur : Ego palam locutus sum mundo ; ego semper docui in synagoga et in templo, quo omnes Judæi conveniunt, et in occulto locutus sum nihil. Hinc subditur : In plateis dat vocem suam : quia in latitudinibus viarum ac gentium prædicavit per suos ministros : quibus commisit, Quæ auditis in aure, prædicate super tecta. Nempe, ut fassus est, Qui facit veritatem, venit ad lucem. Nec his obstat, quod de Christo prædictum est, Non clamabit, nec audietur foris vox ejus : quia per hoc, non nisi irrationabilis et indecens clamor de ipso negatur. Unde jubet Apostolus : Omnis amaritudo, et indignatio, et ira, et clamor tollatur a vobis.
paras.en: Next it is shown that no one can be excused by ignorance for his unbelief. [[1:20|Wisdom preacheth abroad|Sapientia foris prædicat]]. This can be taken of the uncreated Wisdom, who is Christ the Lord, the eternal Word of God the Father[[1 Cor 1:24||]][[1 Cor 1:30||]], who preached abroad, that is, among the gentiles and the faithless.
